content: 1. Even up to two months after discontinuing the antibiotic, you should remain vigilant for symptoms of certain conditions. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in your stool, severe stomach cramps, or a fever that begins after starting or stopping the medication. 2. Oxacillin can cause blood disorders, including eosinophilia, agranulocytosis, neutropenia, and bone marrow suppression. Stop using oxacillin and seek medical attention immediately if you experience symptoms such as fever, shortness of breath, pale or yellowish skin, easy bruising or bleeding, frequent infections, unusual weakness or fatigue, dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting, headache, or an abnormally fast or irregular heartbeat. 3. Liver damage, also known as hepatotoxicity, can occur with the use of oxacillin. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience nausea, vomiting, stomach or abdominal pain, fever, weakness, unusual tiredness, itching, loss of appetite, light-colored stool, dark-colored urine, or yellowing of the skin or the whites of your eyes (jaundice). 4. Individuals who are allergic to oxacillin or any of its ingredients should not use this medication. Your pharmacist can provide a complete list of ingredients in the specific oxacillin product you are prescribed. 5. Oxacillin is typically administered by a healthcare provider in a hospital or clinic setting. If you store oxacillin at home, do not share it with others, even if they have the same condition, as it may harm them. Keep oxacillin out of the reach of children. 6. Before using oxacillin, inform your healthcare provider about all your health conditions and any prescription or over-the-counter medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, or other supplements you are taking. This information will help your provider determine if oxacillin is appropriate for you. Specifically, discuss any allergies to penicillin, other medications, corn, or corn products, as well as any history of asthma, liver problems, kidney problems, or antibiotic-associated diarrhea. 7. Oxacillin may interact with other medications and supplements. Inform your healthcare provider if you are using any tetracyclines (e.g., tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline, omadacycline, sarecycline) or probenecid, a medication commonly used for gout. This may not be a complete list of potential drug interactions. 8. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, inform your healthcare provider. It is not known if or how oxacillin could affect pregnancy or harm an unborn baby. Your provider will advise you on whether you should use oxacillin during pregnancy. 9. If you are breastfeeding or planning to breastfeed, inform your healthcare provider. Oxacillin passes into breast milk, and your provider will guide you on its use while nursing. 10. There are no known interactions between oxacillin and foods or drinks. However, it is unclear if alcohol consumption affects oxacillin. Heavy drinking can weaken your immune response and make it harder for your body to fight infections. 11. If you or someone else accidentally uses too much oxacillin, seek medical help immediately. Call 911 or contact a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. 12. If you miss a dose of oxacillin, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take only the next scheduled dose. Do not take double or extra doses. It is important to complete the full prescribed course of oxacillin, even if your symptoms improve or resolve, to reduce the risk of future infections becoming resistant to oxacillin or similar medications.
